ann_110.text: In this part, an international plan clearly raises the predicted chance for a typical customer from about 12% to about 65%, and a voice-mail plan clearly lowers it to about 2%.
More voice-mail messages raise it steadily, from about 12% at 0 messages to about 44% at 32 messages (on the training data only).

State shifts it in this part (on the training data only): up to about 33% in Washington, about 21% in Texas, Nevada and Maine and about 17% to 18% in North Carolina, Kentucky, Utah and Minnesota, and down to about 2% in Hawaii, 4% in Vermont and 6% in California.

Smaller effects, each changing the predicted chance only slightly (on the training data only): most other states shift it by a few points either way; more international calls lower it steadily, each extra call taking off about the same; more evening minutes also lower it steadily; a longer account and more night-time calls raise it steadily.

ann_111.text: This part acts on 661 of 4000 customers, and 267 of them left.

For a typical customer it acts on (in New Jersey, with about 241 daytime minutes costing about $41 and 228 evening minutes), it clearly raises the predicted chance that a customer leaves from about 27% to about 82%.

For that customer, a higher evening charge clearly raises it in an uneven way, from about 27% at $11.76 to about 95% at $22.57, and more night-time minutes clearly raise it in an uneven way, from about 42% at 136 minutes to about 93% at 264 minutes.
More voice-mail messages clearly lower it in an uneven way, from about 82% at 0 messages to about 27% at 32 messages.

For a typical customer, a higher daytime charge clearly raises it in an uneven way, and even more so if the evening charge is above about $17 (about 12% to 72%, against 12% to 16%) or night-time minutes are above 200 (about 12% to 62%, against 12% to 26%), but only for customers with no voice-mail messages.
The daytime charge clearly adds to it only once it rises above about $40, in an uneven way across customers: going from $0 to $46 moves a typical such customer from about 12% to about 81%.

ann_112.text: This part acts on 647 of 4000 customers, and 167 of them left.

For a typical customer it acts on (three calls to customer service and about 135 daytime minutes costing about $23), it clearly raises the predicted chance that a customer leaves from about 12% to about 24%.

For that customer, more daytime minutes clearly lower it in an uneven way, from about 35% at 112 minutes to about 12% at 249 minutes, and going from 0 to 3 customer-service calls clearly raises it in an uneven way, from about 12% to about 24%.
Customer-service calls clearly add to it from about 4 calls upwards, in an uneven way across customers: going from 0 to 4 calls moves a typical customer from about 12% to about 26%.
More night-time minutes barely change it, and being in Idaho or Montana lowers it only slightly (on the training data only).

ann_113.text: This part acts on only 2 of 4000 customers, both of whom left.
One small part barely changes the predictions.

ann_114.text: Calls to customer service clearly add to the predicted chance from about 3 calls upwards: going from 0 to 4 calls moves a typical customer from about 12% to about 18%.

This part acts on 757 of 4000 customers (172 of them left), and for a typical one, in Idaho with three customer-service calls, it raises the predicted chance only slightly, from about 13% to about 14%.
Being in Virginia or South Carolina changes the predicted chance only slightly here.
Customer-service calls add nothing here until about 3 calls, then steadily, so going from 0 to 3 calls changes it only slightly.
A higher daytime charge and more evening minutes barely change it, lowering it only slightly (on the training data only).

What the daytime charge does here comes only once it rises above about $44, mostly in a jump around $43 to $44 where this part switches on, and it lowers the predicted chance only slightly (on the training data only).

ann_115.text: A higher international charge raises the predicted chance slowly at first, then faster: for a typical customer, from about 12% at $1.84 to about 18% at $3.70, and it adds to it only once the charge rises above about $2.87 (on the training data only).
The effect of international charge is clearly larger for customers in California: from about 26% to about 58%, against about 12% to 18% in states other than New York, California and Tennessee.
Through this part, being in California raises the predicted chance from about 12% to about 45% (on the training data only).
Being in Tennessee raises it only slightly, to about 16% (on the training data only).
This part acts on 1867 of 4000 customers, and for a typical one (in Idaho) it raises the predicted chance only slightly, from about 13% to about 15% (on the training data only).

ann_116.text: Through this part, being in New Jersey raises the predicted chance for a typical customer from about 12% to about 21%, and being in California raises it to about 18% (on the training data only).
Being in Oklahoma, New York or Massachusetts changes it only slightly (on the training data only).

ann_117.text: A longer account adds nothing here until about 131, then steadily, so going from 48 to 152 raises the predicted chance only slightly in this part (on the training data only).
For a typical customer it stays at about 12%.

ann_118.text: Calls to customer service clearly add to the predicted chance from about 3 calls upwards, in an uneven way across customers: going from 0 to 4 calls moves a typical customer from about 12% to about 36%.

Going from 0 to 3 calls, more daytime minutes, and being in Idaho, Montana, South Carolina or Virginia each change the predicted chance only slightly in this part, the calls and minutes in an uneven way across customers.
More evening and night-time minutes and a higher daytime charge barely change it here, lowering it only slightly (on the training data only).

What the daytime charge does here comes only once it rises above about $44, mostly in a jump around $43 to $44 where this part switches on, and it lowers the predicted chance only slightly (on the training data only).

ann_119.text: Across the whole model, an international plan (about 12% to 65%) and a higher daytime charge from $19 to $42 (about 12% to 43%, in an uneven way across customers) clearly raise the predicted chance that a typical customer leaves, and a voice-mail plan clearly lowers it to about 2%.

State moves it a lot (on the training data only): from about 12% in West Virginia up to about 41% in California, 33% in Washington, 28% in New Jersey and 22% in Tennessee, and down to about 2% in Hawaii and 4% in Vermont.
A higher total international charge raises it slowly at first, then faster, from about 12% at $1.84 to about 18% at $3.70 (on the training data only).
Customers in Texas, Nevada, Maine, Massachusetts, North Carolina, Kentucky, Utah and Minnesota get between about 17% and 21% (on the training data only).

Smaller effects, each changing the predicted chance only slightly (on the training data only): most other states shift it by less than 5 points; more international calls lower it steadily, each extra call taking off about the same; more evening minutes also lower it steadily; more night-time calls raise it steadily; a longer account raises it slowly at first, then faster.

On their own, going from 0 to 3 customer-service calls, daytime minutes, evening charge and night-time minutes change the predicted chance only slightly for a typical customer, each in an uneven way across customers.
It ignores area code, total daytime calls, total evening calls, total international minutes and total night-time charge.

ann_110.original: HYPOTHESIS: a linear logit term (identity node linearSum) over 32 direct inputs. Per SD: internationalPlan +0.77 (+2.64 logit for the 380 holders), voiceMailPlan -0.75, numberVmailMessages +0.74 (partly cancels the plan), totalIntlCalls -0.19, totalEveMinutes -0.12, accountLength +0.08, totalNightCalls +0.02, and 25 state offsets; the large ones are state:11 -2.18 logit (73 rows, 3 churners), state:46 -1.63 (80 rows, 5), state:4 -1.04 direct (41 rows; outweighed by +2.17 via hidden units), state:47 +0.92 (72 rows, 21), state:39 -0.86 (82 rows, 5). EVIDENCE (train, n=4000): closed form exact-affine (formula max err 0.003 from coefficient rounding); sensitivities equal the weights. Rare-category comparison (logit effect vs raw log-odds offset vs calibrating offset after a -1.875 global shift): state:11 -2.18 / -1.36 / -2.37; state:46 -1.63 / -0.92 / -1.81; state:47 +0.92 / +0.94 / +1.19. These state offsets roughly match the calibrating offsets given the other features (fitted rare-category switches, not obviously over-shot on train). Removing all state one-hots costs 0.0055 train AUC.
ann_110.proposed: A straight-line part: an international plan and voice-mail messages raise the predicted chance, a voice-mail plan lowers it, and each state shifts it up or down.

ann_111.original: HYPOTHESIS: a total-usage hinge for customers without voicemail messages. 10110 = relu(1.36*dayCharge + 0.69*eveCharge + 0.40*nightMin - 1.30*vmailMessages - 1.88), output weight +2.82. vmailMessages has z = -0.59 when 0 and >= +1.5 for message users, so any message use pushes the hinge almost entirely off. EVIDENCE (train): closed form exact (relu of affine). Sensitivities dayCharge 0.23, vmail 0.21, eveCharge 0.11, nightMin 0.07. Logit contribution / churn by usage score s=1.36 day+0.69 eve+0.40 night (z): no messages: s<1 0 / 5-11%; [1,1.5) +0.31 / 7%; [1.5,2) +1.67 / 8% (onset too early: an over-shoot on 202 rows); [2,2.5) +3.16 / 67%; >=2.5 +5.88 / 99%. With messages: <=+0.25 at every level, churn 4-10%. Linearising this leaf costs 0.8815 vs full 0.9243 (linear-fit R2 0.3698); restoring it alone onto the fully linearised model gains 0.0708 AUC: the single largest source of nonlinear performance (Shapley share 0.057 of 0.091).
ann_111.proposed: For customers with no voice-mail messages, high combined daytime, evening and night-time usage raises the predicted chance steeply once the daytime charge passes about $40; voice-mail messages switch this off.

ann_112.original: HYPOTHESIS: customer-service calls counted only for low-day-usage customers. 104 = relu(0.687*csc - 0.556*dayMin - 0.856 + 0.041*2546), output +2.27 (via cscSum). 2546 = relu(0.058*csc - 0.875*state:13 - 0.264*state:26 - 0.074*nightMin + 0.117*12106 - 0.942) is active on 8 rows only and its effect on 104 is <= 0.011: a near-inert modulator; 12106 = relu(1.02*csc + 0.81*dayMin - 0.18) only feeds 2546. EVIDENCE (train): closed form (max err 0.001). One call = 0.766 z, so 104 opens at about 1.25 + 0.81*dayMin(z) calls above mean. Gate contribution / churn: 4 calls & day z<-1 +2.87 / 95% (n=21); 4 calls & day z in [-1,0) +1.55 / 62% (74); 4 calls & day z in [0,1) +0.40 / 14% (71); 5 calls & day<-1 +4.17 / 100%; 6 calls & day<-1 +5.30 / 100%; over-shoot at 3 calls & day<-1: +1.70 but churn 6% (n=68). Linearising it alone costs 0.013 AUC; restoring it alone onto the linearised model gains 0.046.
ann_112.proposed: Customer-service calls raise the predicted chance from about 4 calls upwards, and more daytime minutes lower it for the customers this part acts on.

ann_113.original: HYPOTHESIS: 4906 = relu(0.275*csc - 1.51), output +1.55: an extreme-calls hinge (opens at csc z > 5.5, i.e. 9 calls). ann_114.original: HYPOTHESIS: a service-call hinge that is switched off for heavy day+evening users and for state:45. 10992 = relu(0.365*csc - 0.791*state:45 - 1.74*5611 - 0.503), output +1.67. 7701 = relu(1.31*dayCharge + 0.86*eveMin - 0.52) and 5611 = relu(0.80*7701 - 1.16) (on 423 rows, churn 55%) supply the veto. ann_119.proposed: The predicted chance that a customer leaves rises most with an international plan and a high daytime charge, falls with a voice-mail plan, rises from about 3 customer-service calls upwards, shifts by state, and ignores area code and the number of daytime and evening calls.

summary.text: For a typical customer (in West Virginia, area code 415, with no international or voice-mail plan, one call to customer service and median usage, such as about 180 daytime minutes costing about $31), having an international plan clearly raises the predicted chance that a customer leaves from about 12% to about 65%, and having a voice-mail plan clearly lowers it to about 2%.
A higher total daytime charge clearly raises it, in an uneven way across customers: for a typical customer, from about 12% at about $19 to about 43% at about $42.
The rise with daytime charge is clearly much larger when the evening charge is above about $17 (about 12% to 72%, against 12% to 16%), and it happens only for customers with no voice-mail messages.

Calls to customer service clearly add to the predicted chance from about 3 calls upwards, in an uneven way across customers: going from 0 to 4 calls moves a typical customer from about 12% to about 36%.
The state also moves it (on the training data only): customers in California get about 41% and customers in Hawaii about 2%, against 12% in West Virginia.
The model ignores area code, the number of daytime and evening calls, total international minutes and total night-time charge.

parts.original_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: churn logit = -2.164 + linearBackbone + 2.82*heavyUsageNoVmail + serviceCalls + intlChargeHinges + stateUnits + accountLengthHinge, an additive (parallel) composition in the output pre-activation; output = sigmoid. 25 unconnected inputs (incl. totalDayCalls, totalEveCalls, totalIntlMinutes, totalNightCharge, area codes and 17 states) are zero-effect entries. EVIDENCE (train, n=4000, local ablation): full AUC 0.9243 (L2 logistic regression 0.8433). All nonlinear children jointly replaced by least-squares linear fits on their own inputs: 0.8333; all hidden mean-ablated: 0.659. The 0.091 nonlinear gain comes from two children: heavyUsageNoVmail (restore alone +0.0708, Shapley 0.057) and serviceCalls (+0.0489, Shapley 0.035); restoring both gives 0.9244 (= full). intlChargeHinges, stateUnits and accountLengthHinge contribute nothing over their linear fits. The model is miscalibrated on train (mean p 0.336 vs base rate 0.1415; global shift -1.875 needed). Rare-category effects are constant offsets: state:11 -2.18, state:46 -1.63, state:4 +1.12 (mixed direct/hidden, range -0.53..+1.48), state:47 +0.92, state:39 -0.86, state:31 +0.70, state:45 off-switch of the call veto.
variables: number of calls to customer service

parts.name: heavyUsageNoVmail
parts.original_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: a total-usage hinge for customers without voicemail messages. 10110 = relu(1.36*dayCharge + 0.69*eveCharge + 0.40*nightMin - 1.30*vmailMessages - 1.88), output weight +2.82. vmailMessages has z = -0.59 when 0 and >= +1.5 for message users, so any message use pushes the hinge almost entirely off. EVIDENCE (train): closed form exact (relu of affine). Sensitivities dayCharge 0.23, vmail 0.21, eveCharge 0.11, nightMin 0.07. Logit contribution / churn by usage score s=1.36 day+0.69 eve+0.40 night (z): no messages: s<1 0 / 5-11%; [1,1.5) +0.31 / 7%; [1.5,2) +1.67 / 8% (onset too early: an over-shoot on 202 rows); [2,2.5) +3.16 / 67%; >=2.5 +5.88 / 99%. With messages: <=+0.25 at every level, churn 4-10%. Linearising this leaf costs 0.8815 vs full 0.9243 (linear-fit R2 0.3698); restoring it alone onto the fully linearised model gains 0.0708 AUC: the single largest source of nonlinear performance (Shapley share 0.057 of 0.091).

parts.name: linearBackbone
parts.original_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: a linear logit term (identity node linearSum) over 32 direct inputs. Per SD: internationalPlan +0.77 (+2.64 logit for the 380 holders), voiceMailPlan -0.75, numberVmailMessages +0.74 (partly cancels the plan), totalIntlCalls -0.19, totalEveMinutes -0.12, accountLength +0.08, totalNightCalls +0.02, and 25 state offsets; the large ones are state:11 -2.18 logit (73 rows, 3 churners), state:46 -1.63 (80 rows, 5), state:4 -1.04 direct (41 rows; outweighed by +2.17 via hidden units), state:47 +0.92 (72 rows, 21), state:39 -0.86 (82 rows, 5). EVIDENCE (train, n=4000): closed form exact-affine (formula max err 0.003 from coefficient rounding); sensitivities equal the weights. Rare-category comparison (logit effect vs raw log-odds offset vs calibrating offset after a -1.875 global shift): state:11 -2.18 / -1.36 / -2.37; state:46 -1.63 / -0.92 / -1.81; state:47 +0.92 / +0.94 / +1.19. These state offsets roughly match the calibrating offsets given the other features (fitted rare-category switches, not obviously over-shot on train). Removing all state one-hots costs 0.0055 train AUC.

parts.name: serviceCalls
parts.original_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: additive (parallel) composition at identity node cscSum = 2.27*cscLowDayGate + 1.55*cscHighHinge + 1.67*cscVetoedByUsage; the three leaves share only the service-call input (split into copies) and never feed each other. numberCustomerServiceCalls has no direct output edge, so this block is its only route. Together: 0-2 calls ~0 logit (except +0.49 at 2 calls and day z<-1); 4 calls with below-average day usage +2.0..+3.4 logit (churn 62-95%); 4+ calls with heavy usage ~+0.3..+0.6 (churn 33%, the heavy-usage hinge takes over). EVIDENCE (train): closed form exact sum; mean-ablation AUC 0.8343; linearising the block costs 0.0202; restoring it alone onto the linearised model gains 0.0489 (Shapley share 0.035).
variables: number of calls to customer service

parts.name: cscLowDayGate
parts.original_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: customer-service calls counted only for low-day-usage customers. 104 = relu(0.687*csc - 0.556*dayMin - 0.856 + 0.041*2546), output +2.27 (via cscSum). 2546 = relu(0.058*csc - 0.875*state:13 - 0.264*state:26 - 0.074*nightMin + 0.117*12106 - 0.942) is active on 8 rows only and its effect on 104 is <= 0.011: a near-inert modulator; 12106 = relu(1.02*csc + 0.81*dayMin - 0.18) only feeds 2546. EVIDENCE (train): closed form (max err 0.001). One call = 0.766 z, so 104 opens at about 1.25 + 0.81*dayMin(z) calls above mean. Gate contribution / churn: 4 calls & day z<-1 +2.87 / 95% (n=21); 4 calls & day z in [-1,0) +1.55 / 62% (74); 4 calls & day z in [0,1) +0.40 / 14% (71); 5 calls & day<-1 +4.17 / 100%; 6 calls & day<-1 +5.30 / 100%; over-shoot at 3 calls & day<-1: +1.70 but churn 6% (n=68). Linearising it alone costs 0.013 AUC; restoring it alone onto the linearised model gains 0.046.
variables: number of calls to customer service

parts.name: intlChargeHinges
parts.original_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: convex hinges on international charge, shifted on for state:4. 791 = relu(0.995*intlCharge + 0.357*state:4 + 0.132*state:42 + 0.23*8286 - 0.069), output +0.25; 11938 = relu(0.857*791 - 0.348), output +0.37. 8286 = relu(-1.49*state:34 - 0.415) and 14725 = relu(-0.179*11938 - 0.229) are dead (pre-activation < 0 on the whole input domain; active on 0 rows). EVIDENCE (train): closed form (max err 0.004). Sensitivities intlCharge 0.46/0.26, state:4 0.17/0.09, state:42 0.06/0.03. Contribution / churn by intlCharge z: <0 +0.02 / 12%; [0,1) +0.14 / 13%; [1,2) +0.60 / 22%; >=2 +1.23 / 20%. On the 41 state:4 rows the +3.5 shift turns both hinges on (part of state:4's +2.17 hidden-path effect); on state:42 (68 rows) up to +0.58. Although the fit to a line is imperfect (R2 0.7187), linearising costs nothing (0.9244); restore gain -0.0011.

parts.name: cscVetoedByUsage
parts.original_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: a service-call hinge that is switched off for heavy day+evening users and for state:45. 10992 = relu(0.365*csc - 0.791*state:45 - 1.74*5611 - 0.503), output +1.67. 7701 = relu(1.31*dayCharge + 0.86*eveMin - 0.52) and 5611 = relu(0.80*7701 - 1.16) (on 423 rows, churn 55%) supply the veto. EVIDENCE (train): closed form (max err 0.026 from rounding of nested weights). Contribution at calls 3/4/5/6/7: +0.03/+0.5/+0.9/+1.4/+1.9 for average usage. Among 4+ call customers: 7701 off (n=207): veto unit +0.77, churn 65%; 7701 in (1.45,2.5) (n=31): +0.34; 7701 > 2.5 (n=9): 0 (heavy users are already scored by heavyUsageNoVmail, +6.8). state:45 (91 rows, 6 churners) is a hard off switch: its effect ranges -1.43..-0.46 logit. Linearising costs 0.0023 AUC; restoring alone onto the linearised model gains 0.0163.
variables: number of calls to customer service

parts.name: stateUnits
parts.original_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: per-state offset units, each a ReLU of a single one-hot (or two), hence exactly affine in the one-hots on the data. 2181 state:36 (79 rows, -0.27 logit; state:35 weight inert), 2782 state:31 (90 rows, +0.70), 3979->10180->6353 state:4 (41 rows, +0.52 via the always-on relays), 31792 state:34 (93 rows, -0.09), 32184->34043 state:19 (86 rows, +0.21); 5071 = relu(0.0037*state:0 - 0.254) is dead. EVIDENCE (train): closed form (max err 0.005); sensitivities nonzero only for the one-hots; linear fit R2 1.000, linearising costs 0.0000 AUC, mean-ablation costs 0.0009. state:31 +0.70 equals its raw log-odds offset +0.69 (calibrating offset after global shift +0.58).

parts.name: accountLengthHinge
parts.original_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: 15584 = relu(0.946*accountLength - 0.73), output +0.08: a small hinge for long accounts (z > 0.77, 881 rows). EVIDENCE: closed form exact; contribution sd 0.025 logit; ablation changes AUC by 0.0002, linearising by 0.0000.

parts.name: cscHighHinge
parts.original_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: 4906 = relu(0.275*csc - 1.51), output +1.55: an extreme-calls hinge (opens at csc z > 5.5, i.e. 9 calls). EVIDENCE: active on 2 train rows (both churners), max contribution +0.09 logit, sensitivity 0.0001; linearising or ablating changes AUC by < 0.0001. Effectively inert.
variables: number of calls to customer service

reference_patient.definition: the typical patient: the median training patient for every number and the most common training category for every category (not a real patient)

confidence_rules.clearly: a meaningful change in predicted risk for a typical patient (at least 5% points), the test split agrees (same sign, and its bootstrap interval over test patients excludes no benefit), and every group has at least 20 training patients
confidence_rules.consistently across patients: the claim holds for at least 90% of training patients (range across patients); this is not a significance statement
confidence_rules.on the training data only: the test split disagrees (opposite sign, or no benefit on test patients) or is unclear (its interval includes no benefit), or no test check is available
confidence_rules.slightly: the change in predicted risk for a typical patient is below 5% points
confidence_rules.the model has little data on this: a compared group has fewer than 20 training patients

settings.effect_scale: log-odds (output pre-activation) for verification; predicted risk for the typical patient for wording

In the training data, 267 of these 661 customers had churn.

A higher total daytime charge clearly raises the predicted chance that a customer leaves, and even more so if total evening charge is above 17.12 US dollars (in an uneven way for patients with total evening charge above 17.12 US dollars): for a typical customer, total daytime charge going from 19.07 US dollars to 42.40 US dollars moves the predicted chance that a customer leaves from about 12% to about 72% if total evening charge is above 17.12 US dollars, and from about 12% to about 16% if total evening charge is at or below 17.12 US dollars.

Other effects: total daytime charge past about 39.93 US dollars raises it in an uneven way; a higher total evening charge raises it in an uneven way; a higher voice-mail messages lowers it in an uneven way; a higher total night-time minutes raises it in an uneven way; total daytime charge depending on total night-time minutes raises it in an uneven way; a higher total daytime charge raises it in an uneven way; total daytime charge depending on voice-mail messages raises it in an uneven way.

summary.text: For a typical customer, the model gives a clearly higher predicted chance that a customer leaves if the customer has an international plan (about 65%) than if the customer has no international plan (about 12%).

The model treats a higher total daytime charge as clearly raising the predicted chance that a customer leaves in an uneven way: for a typical customer, it goes from about 12% at 19.07 US dollars to about 43% at 42.40 US dollars, flattening out near the top because the predicted risk cannot go much higher.

For a typical customer, the model gives a higher predicted chance that a customer leaves if the customer is in California (about 41%) than if the customer is in West Virginia (about 12%) (on the training data only).

Through one part of the model, total daytime charge only clearly adds to the predicted chance that a customer leaves once it rises above about 39.93 US dollars (between 32.28 US dollars and 53.10 US dollars for different customers): for a typical such customer, going from 0.00 US dollars to 46.09 US dollars moves it from about 12% to about 81%; across patients the change happens in an uneven way.

A higher total international charge clearly raises the predicted chance that a customer leaves, and even more so if the customer is in California (steadily for customers in California): for a typical customer, total international charge going from 1.84 US dollars to 3.70 US dollars moves the predicted chance that a customer leaves from about 26% to about 58% if the customer is in California, and from about 12% to about 18% if state is something other than New York, California, Tennessee.
The model ignores area code, total daytime calls, total evening calls, total international minutes and total night-time charge.
